chapters.title: Unit 1: Cellular Organization of Plants and Animals

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A cell is the structural and functional unit of living organisms.
  • Muscle is a tissue: cells of the same kind group together to perform one function and make a tissue.
  • The circulatory system transports digested food to all parts of the body.
  • The nucleus controls all the activities of the cell, just as the brain controls the body.
  • Centrioles are present in animal cells; plants prepare food in their chloroplasts.
  • Euglena is a unicellular organism; it can be seen clearly with a microscope.
  • Mitochondria are called the power house of the cell.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Fill in the blanks:

Q: 1. A cell is the ______ and functional unit of living organisms.

Ans: structural

Q: 2. Centriole is present in ______ cell.

Ans: animal

Q: 3. Cell membrane is the outer most covering in ______ cells.

Ans: animal

Q: 4. Euglena is a ______ organism.

Ans: unicellular

Q: 5. Plants prepare food in their ______.

Ans: chloroplast

Exercise B: Choose the correct answer:

Q: 1. Muscle is a type of ______.

Options: (a) cell (b) tissue (c) organ (d) system

Correct answer: tissue

Q: 2. A branch on a stem is a part of ______ system.

Options: (a) root (b) branch (c) shoot (d) conducting

Correct answer: shoot

Q: 3. Which system of your body is responsible for the transport of digested food?

Options: (a) digestive system (b) circulatory system (c) respiratory system (d) skeletal system

Correct answer: circulatory system

Q: 4. Brain controls the body just like the ______ controls activities of a cell.

Options: (a) mitochondria (b) cytoplasm (c) nucleus (d) ribosomes

Correct answer: nucleus

Q: 5. Which instrument can help to see amoeba clearly?

Options: (a) hand lens (b) microscope (c) telescope (d) both b and c

Correct answer: microscope

Exercise C: Match Column A with Column B:

Q: 1. Vacuole

Ans: store waste material of cells

Q: 2. Mitochondria

Ans: power house of the cell

Q: 3. Nucleus

Ans: control cell activities

Q: 4. Chloroplast

Ans: help in food preparation

Q: 5. Cell wall

Ans: outer layer of plant cell

mcqs.q: Muscle is a type of ______.
mcqs.why: Many cells of the same kind join together to perform one job. Muscle is made of many muscle cells working together, so muscle is a tissue, not a single cell, an organ or a system.

mcqs.q: A branch on a stem is a part of ______ system.
mcqs.why: The part of the plant above the ground — the stem, its branches and the leaves — is the shoot system. A branch grows on the stem, so it is a part of the shoot system.

mcqs.q: Which system of your body is responsible for the transport of digested food?
mcqs.why: The circulatory system (heart and blood vessels) carries the digested food, dissolved in the blood, to all parts of the body. The digestive system only breaks the food down.

mcqs.q: Brain controls the body just like the ______ controls activities of a cell.
mcqs.why: The nucleus is the control centre of the cell: it controls all the activities of the cell, just as the brain controls the whole body.

mcqs.q: Which instrument can help to see amoeba clearly?
mcqs.why: An amoeba is a microscopic unicellular organism, far too small to be seen clearly with a hand lens. Only a microscope magnifies it enough. (The book's printed fourth option 'both b and c' is replaced here by 'binoculars', because a telescope is used for distant objects and cannot show an amoeba.)

mcqs.q: A cell is the ______ and functional unit of living organisms.
mcqs.why: Every living body is built of cells and every life activity takes place inside cells, so the cell is called the structural and functional unit of living organisms.

mcqs.q: Centriole is present in ______ cell.
mcqs.why: Centrioles are small bodies near the nucleus that take part in cell division. They are present in animal cells and are absent in plant cells.

mcqs.q: Euglena is a ______ organism.
mcqs.why: The whole body of Euglena is made of only one cell, and that one cell performs all the life activities. Such an organism is called unicellular.

mcqs.q: Plants prepare food in their ______.
mcqs.why: Chloroplasts are the green bodies in plant cells that contain chlorophyll. Plants prepare their food by photosynthesis inside the chloroplasts.

mcqs.q: Which cell part is called the power house of the cell?
mcqs.why: Mitochondria produce energy for the cell from food, so they are called the power house of the cell. The vacuole stores material and the nucleus controls the cell.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An animal cell is bounded by the cell membrane; a plant cell also has a hard cell wall outside the membrane.
  • Plant cells have chloroplasts and one large central vacuole; animal cells have small vacuoles and centrioles.
  • Organization in a multicellular organism: Cell, then Tissue, then Organ, then Organ System, then Organism.
  • If the respiratory system does not work properly, enough energy is not produced from food and the person feels weak and may suffocate.
  • Parts of a light microscope: eye piece, nose piece, objective lenses, stage, coarse adjustment knob and fine adjustment knob.

Solved Exercises

Exercise D: Label the following diagrams:

Q: 1. Label the diagram of an Animal Cell.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The animal cell is an oval cell bounded by the cell (plasma) membrane, which is its outer most covering. Inside it, the labels are: Vacuole (a small sac-like structure near the top), Mitochondrion (oval bodies that produce energy), Nucleus (the large round body in the centre which controls all activities of the cell), Centrioles (two small bodies near the nucleus, each composed of 9 microtubules, involved in cell division) and Cytoplasm (the jelly-like liquid filling the cell).

Q: 2. Label the diagram of a Plant Cell.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The plant cell is a rectangular cell. Its labels are: Cell wall (the hard outer most covering), Cell membrane (present just under the cell wall), Chloroplast (green bodies containing chlorophyll), Vacuole membrane (the covering of the vacuole), Large central vacuole (the big sac in the centre), Nucleus (the round body on one side), Mitochondrion (energy-producing body) and Cytoplasm (the liquid filling the cell).

Exercise E: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. What will happen to a person whose respiratory system is not working properly?

Ans: The respiratory system helps in the production of energy from the food. If the respiratory system of a person is not working properly, he will not be able to breathe in air properly, so enough energy will not be produced from the food and the person will feel weak and may even suffocate.

Q: 2. Describe basic organization of a multicellular organism.

Ans: In a multicellular organism the organization is: Cell, then Tissue, then Organ, then Organ System, then Organism. Cells which perform the same function group together to make a tissue. Different tissues work together to make an organ. Many organs work together to make a system, and many systems combine to make the organism.

Q: 3. Differentiate between an animal and a plant cell.

Ans: A plant cell has a cell wall which is its outer most covering, but an animal cell has no cell wall and its cell membrane is the outer most covering. A plant cell has chloroplasts and one large central vacuole, while an animal cell has no chloroplast and has small vacuoles. Centrioles are present in animal cells but not in plant cells. Both cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria in common.

Q: 4. Draw the diagram of a microscope and name its different parts.

Ans: Diagram (in words): A light microscope has the following parts. Eye Piece: it magnifies the image many times. Nose Piece: it is turned to change the magnification of objective lenses. Objective Lenses: three lenses with different magnification. Stage: the area on which a slide is placed. Coarse Adjustment Knob: it moves the stage up and down for adjustment. Fine Adjustment Knob: it moves the body tube for sharpening the image. Mirror: it reflects light on the slide.

mcqs.q: What is the outer most covering of an animal cell?
mcqs.why: An animal cell has no cell wall. It is bounded by the thin cell (plasma) membrane, which is its outer most covering.

mcqs.q: What is the outer most covering of a plant cell?
mcqs.why: A plant cell has a hard cell wall outside the cell membrane. The cell wall is the outer most covering of a plant cell and gives it a fixed shape.

mcqs.q: Each centriole in an animal cell is composed of how many microtubules?
mcqs.why: The diagram answer in this unit states that each centriole is composed of 9 microtubules, and the two centrioles near the nucleus are involved in cell division.

mcqs.q: What is the first (lowest) level of organization in a multicellular organism?
mcqs.why: The organization of a multicellular organism starts from the cell: cell, then tissue, then organ, then organ system, and finally the organism.

mcqs.q: Cells which perform the same function group together to make a ______.
mcqs.why: A group of cells of the same kind performing the same function is called a tissue, for example muscle tissue.

mcqs.q: If the respiratory system of a person is not working properly, he may ______.
options: feel weak and may even suffocate
mcqs.why: The respiratory system helps in producing energy from food by taking in air. If it does not work properly, enough energy is not produced, so the person feels weak and may even suffocate.

mcqs.q: How is the vacuole of a plant cell different from that of an animal cell?
options: plant cell has one large central vacuole
animal cell has one large vacuole
mcqs.why: A plant cell has one large central vacuole, while an animal cell has only small vacuoles. Plant cells also have chloroplasts, which animal cells do not have.

mcqs.q: Which part of a microscope magnifies the image many times?
mcqs.why: In a light microscope, the eye piece is the lens at the top through which we look; it magnifies the image many times.

mcqs.q: The stage of a microscope is the area on which ______.
mcqs.why: The stage is the flat area of the microscope on which the slide containing the specimen is placed for observation.

mcqs.q: Many organs work together to make a ______.
mcqs.why: Different tissues make an organ, and many organs working together for one function make an organ system, such as the digestive system.

lessons.title: Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Project Work

Q: Draw the organs involved in the human digestive system and order them in the right sequence on a chart or on a table.

Ans: The organs of the human digestive system in the right sequence are: 1. Mouth, 2. Oesophagus, 3. Stomach, 4. Small intestine, 5. Large intestine, 6. Rectum, 7. Anus. These organs work together for the digestion of food.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Receptor cells present in the sense organs receive stimuli like light, sound, taste and smell.
  • The retina is the layer of the eye that has sensory cells; the optic nerve takes its signals to the brain.
  • The ear drum vibrates when sound waves strike it; hearing is helped by the auditory nerve.
  • The tongue is the organ of taste; the sensations of sour and salty tastes are received on the sides of the tongue.
  • We smell odorous substances through the nose.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Fill in the blanks:

Q: 1. Receptor cells are present in ______ organs.

Ans: sense

Q: 2. The layer of the eye that has sensory cells is called ______.

Ans: retina

Q: 3. Vibration of the ear drum is due to ______ waves.

Ans: sound

Q: 4. The sensation relating to sour and salty tastes are received by receptor cells located on the ______ of the tongue.

Ans: sides

Q: 5. You can smell odorous substances through your ______.

Ans: nose

Exercise B: Select the best answers:

Q: 1. We can sense different stimuli due to

Options: (a) sense organs (b) blood (c) environment (d) nutrition

Correct answer: sense organs

Q: 2. In the eye, sensory cells are located on

Options: (a) choroid (b) sclera (c) iris (d) retina

Correct answer: retina

Q: 3. The optic nerves behind the retina take signals to the

Options: (a) arm (b) brain (c) ear (d) nose

Correct answer: brain

Q: 4. Hearing is helped by

Options: (a) optic nerve (b) auditory nerve (c) sensory nerve (d) motor nerve

Correct answer: auditory nerve

Q: 5. Which organ is used for tasting?

Options: (a) nose (b) ear (c) tongue (d) eye

Correct answer: tongue

mcqs.q: We can sense different stimuli due to ______.
mcqs.why: Stimuli such as light, sound, taste, smell and touch are received by our sense organs — eyes, ears, tongue, nose and skin — so we are able to sense them.

mcqs.q: In the eye, sensory cells are located on ______.
mcqs.why: The retina is the layer of the eye which contains the sensory (light-sensitive) cells. The image of an object is formed on the retina.

mcqs.q: The optic nerves behind the retina take signals to the ______.
mcqs.why: The image formed on the retina is converted into signals, and the optic nerve carries these signals to the brain, which interprets them as sight.

mcqs.q: Hearing is helped by ______.
mcqs.why: The vibrations received by the inner ear are carried to the brain by the auditory nerve, so hearing is helped by the auditory nerve.

mcqs.q: Which organ is used for tasting?
mcqs.why: The tongue has taste buds with receptor cells for sweet, sour, salty and bitter tastes, so the tongue is the organ used for tasting.

mcqs.q: Receptor cells are present in ______ organs.
mcqs.why: Receptor cells are the special cells that receive stimuli from the surroundings. They are present in the sense organs such as the eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin.

mcqs.q: The layer of the eye that has sensory cells is called ______.
mcqs.why: Of all the parts of the eye, only the retina has sensory cells. Light falls on the retina and its sensory cells send the message to the brain.

mcqs.q: Vibration of the ear drum is due to ______ waves.
mcqs.why: Sound waves collected by the outer ear travel through the ear canal and strike the ear drum, which makes the ear drum vibrate.

mcqs.q: The sensations relating to sour and salty tastes are received by receptor cells located on the ______ of the tongue.
mcqs.why: Different parts of the tongue receive different tastes. The receptor cells for sour and salty tastes are located on the sides of the tongue.

mcqs.q: You can smell odorous substances through your ______.
mcqs.why: The nose contains receptor cells for smell. Odorous substances present in the air reach these cells, and we smell them through the nose.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The ear has three parts: outer ear (pinna and ear canal), middle ear (ear drum and three tiny bones called ossicles) and inner ear (semi-circular canals and cochlea).
  • The eye is a hollow, spherical eyeball with three layers; the outer most white layer is the sclerotic (sclera) and its thin transparent front part is the cornea.
  • An inverted image is formed on the retina; the brain interprets it and gives the sensation of an upright image.
  • Bitter taste buds are at the back of the tongue, sour taste buds on the sides and sweet taste buds in the central part.
  • After eating sweets, the sweet receptor cells become less sensitive for some time, so tea seems tasteless.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Label the following diagrams:

Q: 1. Label the diagram of the Human Ear.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The human ear has three main parts. Outer ear: Pinna (the outer funnel-like part that collects sound waves) and Ear canal (the hollow tube leading to the ear drum). Middle ear: Ear drum (the membrane at the end of the ear canal) and the Set of ear bones (three tiny bones called ossicles). Inner ear: Semi-circular canals (which also help in maintaining the balance of the body), Cochlea (the coiled, snail shell shaped structure filled with fluid) and Auditory nerve (which carries the messages to the brain).

Q: 2. Label the diagram of the Human Eye.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The human eye is a hollow, spherical eyeball with three layers. Its labels are: Sclerotic (the outer most white layer, also called sclera), Cornea (the thin transparent front part of the sclerotic layer), Aqueous humour (the fluid behind the cornea), Lens (behind the pupil, attached to muscles), Iris (the coloured part behind the cornea), Pupil (the small opening in the centre of the iris), Choroid (the black middle layer filled with blood vessels), Retina (the inner most layer made of sensory cells), Vitreous humour (the jelly filling the eyeball), Yellow spot (a point on the retina) and Optic nerve (which takes the signals to the brain).

Exercise D: Answer the short questions:

Q: 1. Explain how we see different objects and pictures.

Ans: Light reflects from an object and enters the eye through the cornea. It then passes through the eye lens and is focussed on the retina, where an inverted image of the object is formed. This image is sent to the brain through the optic nerve. The brain interprets it and gives the sensation of an upright image of that object. The brain also works out the size and distance of that object. In this way we see different objects and pictures.

Q: 2. Why do we not feel the taste of a bitter almond till we have chewed it a bit?

Ans: The taste buds for bitter taste are located at the back of the tongue. An unchewed bitter almond does not touch those taste buds, so its chemicals do not react with the taste receptor cells. When we chew it a bit, its juice reaches the back of the tongue and reacts with the bitter taste receptor cells, and only then we feel its bitter taste.

Q: 3. Why do we find tea to be tasteless after we have eaten sweets or candies?

Ans: When we eat sweets or candies, the sweet taste receptor cells of the tongue are strongly stimulated and become used to (less sensitive to) the sweet taste for some time. Tea contains only a little sugar, so after eating sweets its weak sweetness does not produce a clear message to the brain, and we find the tea to be tasteless.

Exercise E: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. Describe the structure of the human eye.

Ans: The human eye consists of an eyeball, which is a hollow and spherical body protected by the eyelid. It consists of three layers. (i) The Sclerotic layer is the outermost white part of the eye; it protects the inner parts. It bulges out to form a thin and transparent structure called the cornea. Behind the cornea is a coloured area called the iris, which has a small opening in its centre called the pupil. Behind the pupil lies a lens attached to muscles. (ii) The Choroid is the middle layer of the eye. It is black in colour and is filled with blood vessels that bring oxygen and nutrients to the eye. (iii) The Retina is the innermost layer of the eyeball. It is made up of sensory cells on which the images of objects are formed. Behind the retina are optic nerves which take the signals to the brain and help us to see objects.

Q: 2. Classify the taste buds on the tongue, on the basis of different tastes.

Ans: On the basis of different tastes, the taste buds on the tongue are classified by the regions where they are located, as shown in the figure of the tongue: the taste buds for bitter taste are at the back of the tongue; the taste buds for sour taste are on the sides of the tongue; the taste buds for sweet taste are in the central part of the tongue; and the taste buds for salty and sweet tastes are at the front tip of the tongue. These taste buds contain the taste receptor cells.

Q: 3. Explain the mechanism of hearing.

Ans: Sound waves are collected by the pinna and carried to the ear canal. When these sound waves strike the ear drum, they cause vibrations in it. These vibrations are passed on to the three tiny bones (ossicles) in the middle ear. The bones transmit the vibrations to the inner ear. When the vibrations enter the cochlea fluid, they set the tiny hairs vibrating. They transmit the sound waves to the brain through the auditory nerve. Thus we hear the sound.

mcqs.q: The function of the pinna of the ear is to ______.
options: keep the balance of the body
mcqs.why: The pinna is the outer, funnel-like part of the ear. It collects sound waves and directs them into the ear canal towards the ear drum.

mcqs.q: The three tiny bones of the middle ear are called ______.
mcqs.why: The middle ear contains a set of three tiny bones called ossicles. They pass the vibrations of the ear drum on to the inner ear.

mcqs.q: Besides taking part in hearing, the semi-circular canals of the inner ear also help in ______.
options: maintaining the balance of the body
mcqs.why: The semi-circular canals in the inner ear take part in hearing and also help in maintaining the balance of the body.

mcqs.q: The outer most white layer of the eye is called ______.
mcqs.why: The eyeball has three layers. The outer most white layer is the sclerotic, also called sclera; it protects the inner parts of the eye.

mcqs.q: The coloured part of the eye is the ______.
mcqs.why: Behind the cornea lies the coloured area of the eye called the iris. The small opening in its centre is the pupil.

mcqs.q: The image formed on the retina of the eye is ______.
mcqs.why: Light passing through the eye lens forms an inverted image on the retina. The brain interprets this image and gives the sensation of an upright object.

mcqs.q: The image formed on the retina is sent to the brain through the ______.
mcqs.why: The optic nerve carries the message of the image from the retina to the brain, where it is interpreted as the sensation of sight.

mcqs.q: The taste buds for bitter taste are located ______.
options: at the tip of the tongue
on the sides of the tongue
at the back of the tongue
in the centre of the tongue
mcqs.why: Bitter taste buds are located at the back of the tongue. That is why an unchewed bitter almond is not tasted until chewing takes its juice to the back of the tongue.

mcqs.q: Why does tea seem tasteless after we have eaten sweets or candies?
options: sweet receptor cells become less sensitive for some time
mcqs.why: Eating sweets strongly stimulates the sweet receptor cells and they become less sensitive for some time. Tea contains only a little sugar, so its weak sweetness produces no clear message and the tea seems tasteless.

mcqs.q: The cornea of the eye is ______.
options: the coloured part of the eye
a thin transparent front part of the sclerotic layer
the opening in the centre of the iris
mcqs.why: The sclerotic layer bulges out at the front to form the cornea, a thin and transparent part through which light enters the eye.

chapters.title: Unit 3: Photosynthesis and Respiration in Plants

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make their own food.
  • Photosynthesis needs sunlight, carbon dioxide, water and chlorophyll; oxygen is given off in this process.
  • The main source of energy is sunlight; during photosynthesis light energy is converted into chemical energy.
  • Stomata are the small pores in the leaves that take in carbon dioxide.
  • The suitable temperature range for photosynthesis is 25 °C to 35 °C.
  • Mesophyll cells of the leaf contain chlorophyll.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Fill in the blanks:

Q: 1. The main source of ______ is sunlight.

Ans: energy

Q: 2. Mesophyll cells contain ______.

Ans: chlorophyll

Q: 3. Epidermal layer in a leaf contain small pores called ______.

Ans: stomata

Q: 4. Normal temperature range for photosynthesis is ______ °C to ______ °C.

Ans: 25 °C to 35 °C

Q: 5. During photosynthesis light energy is converted into ______.

Ans: chemical energy

Exercise B: Choose the correct answer:

Q: 1. Plants make their own food through a process called:

Options: (a) respiration (b) photosynthesis (c) fertilization (d) pollination

Correct answer: photosynthesis

Q: 2. Which of these is not needed in the process of photosynthesis?

Options: (a) sunlight (b) carbon dioxide (c) chlorophyll (d) oxygen

Correct answer: oxygen

Q: 3. The small pores or openings in leaves that take in the carbon dioxide are called ______

Options: (a) stomata (b) lamina (c) phloem (d) petiole

Correct answer: stomata

Q: 4. The suitable range of temperature for photosynthesis is

Options: (a) 5°C to 15°C (b) 15°C to 45°C (c) 25°C to 35°C (d) 10°C to 25°C

Correct answer: 25°C to 35°C

Q: 5. What is given off by the plant during photosynthesis that animals need?

Options: (a) oxygen (b) carbon dioxide (c) chlorophyll (d) water vapours

Correct answer: oxygen

mcqs.q: Plants make their own food through a process called ______.
mcqs.why: Green plants prepare their own food from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll. This food-making process is called photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Which of these is not needed in the process of photosynthesis?
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis needs sunlight, carbon dioxide, water and chlorophyll. Oxygen is not needed for it; oxygen is in fact produced and given off during photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: The small pores or openings in leaves that take in the carbon dioxide are called ______.
mcqs.why: The epidermal layer of a leaf contains small pores called stomata. Carbon dioxide from the air enters the leaf through these stomata for photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: The suitable range of temperature for photosynthesis is ______.
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis takes place best within a normal temperature range of 25 °C to 35 °C, as given in this unit.

mcqs.q: What is given off by the plant during photosynthesis that animals need?
mcqs.why: During photosynthesis plants give off oxygen into the atmosphere. Animals and human beings need this oxygen for breathing.

mcqs.q: The main source of ______ is sunlight.
mcqs.why: Sunlight is the main source of energy for life on Earth. Plants trap this light energy during photosynthesis and change it into chemical energy.

mcqs.q: Mesophyll cells of a leaf contain ______.
mcqs.why: The mesophyll cells inside a leaf contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which traps sunlight for photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: During photosynthesis light energy is converted into ______.
mcqs.why: During photosynthesis the light energy from the sun is converted into chemical energy, which is stored in the food (glucose) prepared by the plant.

mcqs.q: The food prepared by plants during photosynthesis is ______.
mcqs.why: In photosynthesis, plants combine carbon dioxide and water to synthesize their food in the form of glucose, a sugar.

mcqs.q: The raw materials used in photosynthesis are ______.
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil as its raw materials, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, to form glucose and oxygen.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Photosynthesis provides food to the plants themselves and, directly or indirectly, to all animals; oxygen is also produced in it.
  • Photosynthesis occurs in the presence of light and chlorophyll; respiration occurs at all times in animal and plant cells.
  • In photosynthesis glucose is formed; in respiration glucose is broken down and energy is released.
  • If all the stomata of a leaf are closed, carbon dioxide cannot enter the leaf, photosynthesis stops and the plant cannot prepare its food.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. Discuss the importance of photosynthesis as a life supporting process.

Ans: Photosynthesis is a life supporting process. Through it, plants combine carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight to synthesize their food in the form of glucose, so it provides food to the plants themselves and, directly or indirectly, to all animals. Oxygen is also produced in this process; some of it is used by the plant itself and the remaining comes out of the leaves into the atmosphere, and this oxygen is utilized by the animals for their survival. A part of the glucose is used as food by the plant for energy, while the remaining glucose is converted into starch and stored in the stem, roots, fruits and seeds, which animals eat as food.

Q: 2. Explain any three factors needed for photosynthesis.

Ans: Three factors needed for photosynthesis are: (1) Light: light energy from the sun is necessary for photosynthesis; during photosynthesis this energy is converted into chemical energy. Low light intensity slows down the process, and at night or in the dark photosynthesis does not take place. (2) Carbon dioxide: during photosynthesis plants combine carbon dioxide and water to form glucose (food). A sharp increase or decrease in the concentration of carbon dioxide slows down the process. (3) Temperature: a suitable temperature ranging from 25°C to 35°C is required for photosynthesis; temperature below or above this range slows down the process. (Chlorophyll and water are the other essential factors.)

Q: 3. Differentiate between photosynthesis and respiration.

Ans: Photosynthesis occurs in the presence of light and chlorophyll in plant cells, while respiration occurs at all times in animal and plant cells. Photosynthesis requires energy (light) to make sugar (glucose), while respiration releases energy from sugar. In photosynthesis glucose is formed, while in respiration glucose is broken. In photosynthesis carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials, while in respiration carbon dioxide and water are the waste products. In photosynthesis oxygen is given out, while in respiration oxygen is taken in. Photosynthesis occurs only in plant cells, while respiration occurs in all animal and plant cells.

Q: 4. What may happen to a plant if all stomata on its leaves are closed by using wax or vaseline?

Ans: The stomata present at the lower surface of the leaf allow carbon dioxide to enter the leaf for photosynthesis, and they also help in the exchange of gases. If all the stomata are closed by wax or vaseline, carbon dioxide will not enter the leaf, so photosynthesis will stop and the plant will not be able to prepare its food. The exchange of gases will also stop, so the plant will not get energy and may die.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis is a life supporting process because it provides food ______.
options: to plants and, directly or indirectly, to all animals
mcqs.why: Through photosynthesis plants prepare food for themselves, and all animals eat plants or eat other animals that eat plants. So photosynthesis feeds all living things, directly or indirectly.

mcqs.q: The oxygen produced in photosynthesis is released into the atmosphere through the ______.
mcqs.why: Some of the oxygen produced in photosynthesis is used by the plant itself, and the remaining oxygen comes out of the leaves into the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: What happens to photosynthesis when the light intensity is low?
mcqs.why: Light energy from the sun is necessary for photosynthesis. Low light intensity slows down the process, and at night or in the dark photosynthesis does not take place.

mcqs.q: Respiration in cells takes place ______.
options: at all times in animal and plant cells
mcqs.why: Unlike photosynthesis, which needs light and chlorophyll, respiration goes on at all times in both animal and plant cells to release energy from food.

mcqs.q: In respiration, glucose is ______.
mcqs.why: In photosynthesis glucose is formed, while in respiration glucose is broken down and the energy stored in it is released.

mcqs.q: If all the stomata of a leaf are closed by using wax or vaseline, photosynthesis will ______.
options: stop, because carbon dioxide cannot enter the leaf
mcqs.why: Stomata allow carbon dioxide to enter the leaf for photosynthesis and also help in the exchange of gases. If they are sealed with wax, carbon dioxide cannot enter, so photosynthesis stops and the plant cannot prepare its food.

mcqs.q: Besides taking in carbon dioxide, stomata also help in ______.
mcqs.why: The stomata present on the leaf surface allow carbon dioxide to enter the leaf and also help in the exchange of gases between the leaf and the air.

mcqs.q: Which of these factors is needed for photosynthesis?
mcqs.why: The factors needed for photosynthesis include light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll. Without light, photosynthesis cannot take place at all.

mcqs.q: During photosynthesis, carbon dioxide and water are the ______.
mcqs.why: In photosynthesis, carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials; glucose and oxygen are the products formed from them.

mcqs.q: The energy for photosynthesis comes from ______.
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis requires energy in the form of light. This light energy comes from the sun and is converted into chemical energy in the food.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Non-living components of the environment are called abiotic components; the living components are biotic.
  • Green plants are regarded as producers in an environment; animals are the consumers.
  • Mutualism: both organisms are benefitted and neither is harmed. Parasitism: one organism benefits and the other is harmed. Predation: a predator kills and eats its prey.
  • Thar is an example of a desert environment; a tapeworm is a parasite living inside the human body.
  • There are two major types of natural environment.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Fill in the blanks:

Q: 1. Non-living components of environment are called ______ component.

Ans: abiotic

Q: 2. In an environment ______ are regarded as producers.

Ans: green plants

Q: 3. Lion is regarded as a ______ in a predator-prey relationship.

Ans: predator

Q: 4. One of the examples of parasites in human body is ______.

Ans: tapeworm

Q: 5. Bacteria in the ______ of human being is an example of mutualism.

Ans: intestines

Exercise B: Choose the correct answer:

Q: 1. Identify the abiotic component in the following.

Options: (a) lion (b) apple (c) water vapours (d) beetle

Correct answer: water vapours

Q: 2. The relationship between two organisms where both are benefitted and neither is harmed is called ______.

Options: (a) predation (b) parasitism (c) mutualism (d) none of these

Correct answer: mutualism

Q: 3. Thar is an example of ______ environment.

Options: (a) tropical rainforest (b) desert (c) aquatic (d) grassland

Correct answer: desert

Q: 4. Mosquito feeding on human blood is an example of:

Options: (a) predation (b) parasitism (c) mutualism (d) none of these

Correct answer: parasitism

Q: 5. There are ______ major types of natural environment.

Options: (a) five (b) three (c) two (d) four

Correct answer: two

mcqs.q: Identify the abiotic component in the following.
mcqs.why: Abiotic components are the non-living parts of the environment. Lion, apple and beetle are living things, while water vapours are non-living, so they are the abiotic component.

mcqs.q: The relationship between two organisms where both are benefitted and neither is harmed is called ______.
mcqs.why: In mutualism both organisms are benefitted and neither is harmed. (The book's printed fourth option 'none of these' is replaced here by 'competition', in which organisms struggle with each other for food and space.)

mcqs.q: Thar is an example of ______ environment.
mcqs.why: Thar is a hot, dry region with very little rainfall, so it is an example of a desert environment.

mcqs.q: Mosquito feeding on human blood is an example of ______.
mcqs.why: A mosquito feeds on human blood and harms the host. When one organism benefits at the cost of the other, the relationship is parasitism. (The book's printed option 'none of these' is replaced here by 'commensalism'.)

mcqs.q: There are ______ major types of natural environment.
mcqs.why: According to this book, there are two major types of natural environment.

mcqs.q: Non-living components of environment are called ______ component.
mcqs.why: The non-living components of the environment, such as sunlight, air, water and soil, are called abiotic components; the living components are called biotic.

mcqs.q: In an environment ______ are regarded as producers.
mcqs.why: Green plants prepare their own food by photosynthesis, so in an environment they are regarded as the producers. Animals, which eat this food, are the consumers.

mcqs.q: Lion is regarded as a ______ in a predator-prey relationship.
mcqs.why: The animal that hunts and eats another animal is the predator. A lion hunts deer and other animals, so the lion is a predator and the hunted animal is its prey.

mcqs.q: One of the examples of parasites in human body is ______.
mcqs.why: A tapeworm lives inside the human intestines and feeds on the digested food of its host, so it is a parasite living in the human body.

mcqs.q: Bacteria in the ______ of human being is an example of mutualism.
mcqs.why: Certain bacteria live in the intestines of human beings: the bacteria get food and shelter, and the humans benefit by being able to digest the food they eat. Both are benefitted, so this is mutualism.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Environment means everything that surrounds us — all the living and non-living things in the area we live in.
  • Abiotic components include sunlight, air, water, soil, sand, stones, temperature, minerals and rainfall.
  • Living things depend on non-living things: photosynthesis in plants depends on carbon dioxide, sunlight, water and temperature.
  • Rainforests are warm and humid all year with dense vegetation; deserts get less than 250 mm of rain a year and have rare, patchy vegetation.
  • If an environment has no producers, no food will be prepared and the consumers will die of hunger.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. Define environment and identify its abiotic components.

Ans: The area we live in and all the living and non-living things in it constitute our environment; in other words, everything that surrounds us is our environment. Its abiotic (non-living) components include sunlight, air, water, soil, sand, stones, temperature, minerals and rainfall. These are essential for the growth and survival of all living things.

Q: 2. Evaluate the interdependence between living things and non-living things.

Ans: Living things and non-living things depend on each other. The process of photosynthesis in plants depends upon abiotic factors like carbon dioxide, sunlight, water and temperature. Plants produce food for their own use as well as for other animals. The waste material of plants and animals is again used up by the plants, and the cycle goes on. In this way the biotic factors depend on the abiotic factors for survival and growth. Living things also depend on one another: for example, trees provide shelter from weather and enemies to birds, squirrels and monkeys, and also provide them food in the form of fruits, nuts, leaves, bark and roots.

Q: 3. Why does vegetation in tropical rainforests differ from the vegetation in deserts?

Ans: Rainforests receive a lot of rainfall around the year and their climate is warm and humid throughout the year, so they have dense vegetation and many trees grow very close to one another. Deserts are found in dry regions where the total annual rainfall is less than 250 mm; water is scarce and humidity in the air is very low, so vegetation is rare and patchy and plants are spaced apart. That is why vegetation in tropical rainforests differs from the vegetation in deserts.

Q: 4. What will happen to an environment having no producers?

Ans: Producers are the green plants which produce food by photosynthesis, and consumers are the animals which consume food prepared by the producers. If an environment has no producers, no food will be prepared in it. The consumers will get nothing to eat and will die of hunger, and the whole environment will be destroyed, because all living things require energy to live and this energy is obtained from the food made by producers.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an abiotic component of the environment?
mcqs.why: Sunlight is a non-living (abiotic) component of the environment, along with air, water, soil, sand, stones, temperature, minerals and rainfall. These are essential for the growth and survival of all living things.

mcqs.q: Deserts are found in regions where the total annual rainfall is less than ______.
mcqs.why: Deserts are found in dry regions where the total annual rainfall is less than 250 mm; water is scarce and humidity in the air is very low, so vegetation is rare and patchy.

mcqs.q: The climate of tropical rainforests is ______.
options: warm and humid throughout the year
mcqs.why: Rainforests receive a lot of rainfall around the year and their climate is warm and humid throughout the year, so they have dense vegetation and many trees grow very close to one another.

mcqs.q: Producers are the green plants which produce food by ______.
mcqs.why: Producers are the green plants, which produce food by photosynthesis. Consumers are the animals which consume the food prepared by the producers.

mcqs.q: What will happen to an environment having no producers?
options: consumers will make their own food
consumers will get nothing to eat and will die of hunger
mcqs.why: If an environment has no producers, no food will be prepared in it. The consumers will get nothing to eat and will die of hunger, and the whole environment will be destroyed, because all living things need energy which is obtained from food.

mcqs.q: The area we live in and all the living and non-living things in it constitute our ______.
mcqs.why: Everything that surrounds us is our environment: the area we live in and all the living and non-living things in it together constitute the environment.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis in plants depends upon abiotic factors like ______.
options: carbon dioxide, sunlight, water and temperature
mcqs.why: The process of photosynthesis in plants depends upon abiotic factors like carbon dioxide, sunlight, water and temperature. This shows the interdependence between living things and non-living things.

mcqs.q: Vegetation in deserts is ______.
options: rare and patchy, with plants spaced apart
mcqs.why: In deserts water is scarce and humidity in the air is very low, so vegetation is rare and patchy and plants are spaced apart — unlike the dense vegetation of rainforests.

mcqs.q: The waste material of plants and animals is again used up by ______.
mcqs.why: Living things and non-living things depend on each other in a cycle: plants produce food, animals use it, and the waste material of plants and animals is again used up by the plants.

mcqs.q: A cat grabbing and killing a rat, and a lion preying on a deer, are examples of ______.
mcqs.why: In predation, one animal (the predator) grabs, kills and eats another animal (the prey). The project work of this unit lists a cat killing a rat and a lion preying on a deer as examples of predation.

lessons.title: Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Project Work

Q: Find examples of predation, parasitism and mutualism and make a chart of them.

Ans: Predation: a cat grabbing and killing a rat; a lion preying on a deer; a sparrow eating an insect; a tiger preying on a deer. Parasitism: a mosquito feeding on human blood; a tapeworm living inside the human intestines. Mutualism: a certain kind of bacteria living in the intestines of human beings — the bacteria get food and shelter, and the humans benefit by being able to digest the food they eat.

chapters.title: Unit 5: Atoms, Molecules, Mixtures and Compounds

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The symbol used for sodium is Na.
  • Washing soda is a compound of sodium, carbon and oxygen; water is a compound, not a mixture.
  • Chromatography is used to separate coloured substances from each other.
  • In filtration, the particles left behind on the filter paper are called residue.
  • Methane, CH4, has 1 atom of carbon and 4 atoms of hydrogen.
  • Salt is obtained from a mixture of sand, salt and water by dissolving, then filtration, then evaporation.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Select the best answer:

Q: 1. The symbol used for sodium is ______

Options: (a) S (b) Sd (c) Na (d) N

Correct answer: Na

Q: 2. The constituent elements of washing soda are ______

Options: (a) carbon and oxygen (b) sodium and oxygen (c) sodium and carbon (d) sodium, carbon and oxygen

Correct answer: sodium, carbon and oxygen

Q: 3. Which of these is not a mixture?

Options: (a) water (b) air (c) tea (d) alloy

Correct answer: water

Q: 4. Which method is usually used to separate coloured substances from each other?

Options: (a) Simple distillation (b) Evaporation (c) Chromatography (d) Crystallization

Correct answer: Chromatography

Q: 5. The particles left behind on the filter paper in the filtration process are called ______

Options: (a) filtrate (b) residue (c) distillate (d) none of them

Correct answer: residue

Q: 6. Which atoms are found in CH4 (methane)?

Options: (a) 4 carbon and 4 hydrogen (b) 1 carbon and 1 hydrogen (c) 1 carbon and 4 hydrogen (d) 4 carbons and 1 hydrogen

Correct answer: 1 carbon and 4 hydrogen

Q: 7. The correct order for obtaining salt from a mixture of sand, salt and water is:

Options: (a) dissolving - filtration - evaporation (b) evaporation - filtration - dissolving (c) filtration - dissolving - evaporation (d) dissolving - evaporation - filtration

Correct answer: dissolving - filtration - evaporation

mcqs.q: The symbol used for sodium is ______.
mcqs.why: Sodium is represented by the symbol Na (from its Latin name). S is the symbol of sulphur and N is the symbol of nitrogen.

mcqs.q: The constituent elements of washing soda are ______.
mcqs.why: Washing soda is a compound made of three elements joined together: sodium, carbon and oxygen.

mcqs.q: Which of these is not a mixture?
mcqs.why: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen combined chemically in a fixed ratio, so it is not a mixture. Air, tea and alloys are mixtures.

mcqs.q: Which method is usually used to separate coloured substances from each other?
mcqs.why: Chromatography is the method usually used to separate coloured substances, such as the dyes in ink, from each other.

mcqs.q: The particles left behind on the filter paper in the filtration process are called ______.
mcqs.why: In filtration, the insoluble particles that are left behind on the filter paper are called the residue, while the liquid that passes through is the filtrate. (The book's printed fourth option 'none of them' is replaced here by 'sediment'.)

mcqs.q: Which atoms are found in CH4 (methane)?
mcqs.why: In the formula CH4, the letter C stands for carbon with no number after it, which means 1 atom, and H4 means 4 atoms of hydrogen. So methane has 1 carbon atom and 4 hydrogen atoms.

mcqs.q: The correct order for obtaining salt from a mixture of sand, salt and water is:
mcqs.why: First the mixture is dissolved in water so the salt dissolves and the sand does not; then filtration removes the sand; then evaporation drives off the water and leaves the salt. Step 1: dissolving. Step 2: filtration. Step 3: evaporation.

mcqs.q: CO2 (carbon dioxide) has ______.
options: 2 atoms of carbon and 1 atom of oxygen
1 atom of carbon and 2 atoms of oxygen
1 atom of carbon and 1 atom of oxygen
2 atoms of carbon and 2 atoms of oxygen
mcqs.why: In CO2, C has no number after it, so there is 1 atom of carbon, and O2 shows 2 atoms of oxygen.

mcqs.q: From the list oxygen, sea water, calcium, argon, water, air, iron and copper — which are metallic elements?
mcqs.why: Metals are lustrous elements that conduct heat and electricity. From the list, calcium, iron and copper are metallic elements; oxygen and argon are non-metallic elements, and water, air and sea water are not elements at all.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is a compound?
mcqs.why: A compound is formed by the chemical combination of two or more elements in a fixed ratio. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen; brass, air and tea are mixtures.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • CO2 has 1 atom of carbon and 2 atoms of oxygen; H2O has 2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen; sugar, C12H22O11, has 12 carbon, 22 hydrogen and 11 oxygen atoms.
  • Metallic elements: calcium, iron and copper. Non-metallic elements: oxygen, argon, diamond (carbon), sulphur and nitrogen.
  • Compounds: water, carbon monoxide, sodium chloride and ammonia. Mixtures: sea water, air, brass, tea and milk.
  • An element cannot be broken down into a simpler substance; a compound is formed by the chemical combination of two or more elements in a fixed ratio.
  • A mixture is formed by physically combining substances in any proportion; its components keep their properties and can be separated by physical methods.
  • Salt is obtained from salt solution by evaporation: on heating, the water evaporates and solid salt is left behind.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1(i). Carbon dioxide, CO2

Ans: CO2 has 1 atom of carbon and 2 atoms of oxygen.

Q: 1(ii). Water, H2O

Ans: H2O has 2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen.

Q: 1(iii). Methane, CH4

Ans: CH4 has 1 atom of carbon and 4 atoms of hydrogen.

Q: 1(iv). Vinegar, CH3COOH

Ans: CH3COOH has 2 atoms of carbon, 4 atoms of hydrogen and 2 atoms of oxygen.

Q: 1(v). Sugar, C12H22O11

Ans: C12H22O11 has 12 atoms of carbon, 22 atoms of hydrogen and 11 atoms of oxygen.

Q: 2a. From the list (oxygen, sea water, calcium, argon, water, air, carbon monoxide, iron, sodium chloride, diamond, brass, copper, tea, sulphur, milk, nitrogen, ammonia) — which are metallic elements?

Ans: Metallic elements: calcium, iron and copper.

Q: 2b. Which are non-metallic elements?

Ans: Non-metallic elements: oxygen, argon, diamond (carbon), sulphur and nitrogen.

Q: 2c. Which are compounds?

Ans: Compounds: water, carbon monoxide, sodium chloride and ammonia.

Q: 2d. Which are mixtures?

Ans: Mixtures: sea water, air, brass, tea and milk.

Q: 3a. From the list (bromine, carbon dioxide, helium, steel, air, oil, marble, copper, water, sand, tin, bronze, mercury, salt) — which is a solid element?

Ans: A solid element: copper (tin is also a solid element).

Q: 3b. Which is a liquid element?

Ans: A liquid element: bromine (mercury, a metal, is also a liquid at room temperature).

Q: 3c. Which is a gaseous mixture?

Ans: A gaseous mixture: air.

Q: 3d. Which is a solid mixture?

Ans: A solid mixture: steel (bronze and sand are also solid mixtures).

Q: 3e. Which is a liquid compound?

Ans: A liquid compound: water.

Q: 3f. Which is a solid compound?

Ans: A solid compound: salt (sodium chloride).

Q: 3g. Which is a gaseous element?

Ans: A gaseous element: helium.

Q: 3h. Which is a gaseous compound?

Ans: A gaseous compound: carbon dioxide.

Q: 4a. Define: element

Ans: An element is a substance that cannot be broken down into further simpler substance by either chemical or physical methods. It is composed of only one kind of atoms. For example, helium, gold and sodium are all elements.

Q: 4b. Define: metal

Ans: A metal is a substance that is lustrous (shiny) and opaque. Metals can pass electricity and heat (conductors), can be beaten into thin sheets and foils without breaking (malleable), can be drawn into thin wires (ductile), usually melt at high temperature and produce a bell-like sound when struck (sonorous). All metals are solid except mercury. For example, iron, copper, silver and gold.

Q: 4c. Define: non-metal

Ans: Non-metals have a dull surface and low density, except diamond (carbon). They cannot be beaten into thin sheets and foils (non-malleable) and cannot be drawn into thin wires (non-ductile). They cannot pass electricity and heat, except graphite (carbon). They may be solid, liquid or gas. For example, oxygen, sulphur and bromine.

Q: 4d. Define: compound

Ans: Compounds are pure substances which are formed by the chemical combination of two or more different elements in a fixed ratio. For example, water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.

Q: 4e. Define: molecule

Ans: The smallest particle of a substance which can exist independently and shows all the properties of that particular substance is called a molecule. A molecule is formed by the chemical combination of two or more atoms. For example, hydrogen (H2), oxygen (O2), carbon monoxide (CO) and water (H2O) molecules.

Q: 4f. Define: mixture

Ans: A mixture is an impure substance formed when two or more than two substances are physically combined with each other in any proportion. The components of a mixture keep their original properties and can be easily separated by physical means. For example, sugar solution (a mixture of sugar and water) and salt solution (a mixture of salt and water).

Q: 5. Make a list of some common mixtures, stating what they are composed of.

Ans: Some common mixtures and their composition are: Air — a mixture of different gases (nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, carbon dioxide 0.03%, noble gases 0.9% and water vapours). Ice-cream — a mixture of milk, sugar, starch and flavor. Tea — a mixture of water, sugar, tea and milk. Ink — a mixture of different dyes. Alloys — mixtures of different elements, e.g. brass is an alloy of zinc and copper. Sugar solution — a mixture of sugar and water. Salt solution — a mixture of salt and water.

Q: 6. Devise a method for obtaining salt (sodium chloride) from salt solution in the school laboratory.

Ans: Take the salt solution in an evaporating (china) dish and heat it gently in the school laboratory. The water of the solution evaporates on heating, and solid salt (sodium chloride) is left behind in the dish. This method is evaporation to dryness. (If the water is also to be recovered, distillation is used: the solution is heated in a distillation flask, the water vapours are condensed in the condenser and collected as distillate, leaving the salt behind in the flask.)

mcqs.q: H2O (water) has ______.
options: 1 atom of hydrogen and 2 atoms of oxygen
2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen
2 atoms of hydrogen and 2 atoms of oxygen
1 atom of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen
mcqs.why: In H2O, H2 means 2 atoms of hydrogen and O with no number means 1 atom of oxygen.

mcqs.q: Sugar, C12H22O11, has how many atoms of oxygen?
mcqs.why: The number written after the symbol O in C12H22O11 is 11, so one molecule of sugar has 11 atoms of oxygen (and 12 of carbon and 22 of hydrogen).

mcqs.q: Vinegar, CH3COOH, has how many atoms of carbon?
mcqs.why: CH3COOH contains carbon at two places: the C of CH3 and the C of COOH. Adding them, 1 + 1 = 2 atoms of carbon (with 4 atoms of hydrogen and 2 atoms of oxygen).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-metallic element?
mcqs.why: Sulphur has a dull surface, cannot be beaten into sheets or drawn into wires and does not conduct electricity, so it is a non-metallic element. Calcium, iron and copper are metals.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a gaseous mixture?
mcqs.why: Air is a mixture of different gases — nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, carbon dioxide 0.03%, noble gases 0.9% and water vapours — physically combined, so it is a gaseous mixture.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a solid mixture?
mcqs.why: Steel is an alloy, a mixture of iron with other elements, so it is a solid mixture. Copper is an element, salt is a compound and helium is a gaseous element.

mcqs.q: Which element is a liquid at room temperature?
mcqs.why: Bromine is a liquid element (mercury, a metal, is also a liquid at room temperature). Copper and tin are solid elements and helium is a gas.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a gaseous element?
mcqs.why: Helium is a single element that exists as a gas. Carbon dioxide is a gaseous compound, air is a gaseous mixture and water is a liquid compound.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a gaseous compound?
mcqs.why: Carbon dioxide is formed by the chemical combination of carbon and oxygen and exists as a gas, so it is a gaseous compound. Helium and oxygen are elements and air is a mixture.

mcqs.q: An element is a substance that ______.
options: can be broken into many substances
cannot be broken down into a further simpler substance
is formed by mixing two substances
mcqs.why: An element is a substance that cannot be broken down into further simpler substances by either chemical or physical methods. It is composed of only one kind of atoms, for example helium, gold and sodium.

mcqs.q: Metals can be beaten into thin sheets and foils without breaking. This property is called ______.
mcqs.why: Metals are malleable: they can be beaten into thin sheets and foils without breaking. Ductile means they can be drawn into thin wires, and lustrous means they are shiny.

mcqs.q: Non-metals cannot pass electricity and heat, except ______.
mcqs.why: Non-metals are non-conductors, but graphite, a form of carbon, is an exception: it can pass electricity. Diamond, another form of carbon, is an exception in hardness and shine.

mcqs.q: Compounds are pure substances formed by ______.
options: physical mixing of substances in any proportion
the chemical combination of two or more different elements in a fixed ratio
mcqs.why: A compound is formed when two or more different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio, for example water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.

mcqs.q: The smallest particle of a substance which can exist independently and shows all the properties of that substance is called a ______.
mcqs.why: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and shows all the properties of that substance. It is formed by the chemical combination of two or more atoms.

mcqs.q: The components of a mixture keep their original properties and can be separated by ______.
mcqs.why: In a mixture the components are only physically combined and keep their original properties, so they can be easily separated by physical means, for example iron filings are separated from sulphur by a magnet.

lessons.title: Project Work
lessons.notes_html:
Project Work

Q: a(i). Iron filings and sulphur powder are mixed on a paper and a magnet is held over it. What will happen?

Ans: The iron filings will be attracted by the magnet and will stick to it, while the sulphur powder will stay on the paper. In this way the iron filings are separated from the sulphur.

Q: a(ii). What does it show?

Ans: It shows that in a mixture the components are only physically combined and keep their original properties (iron keeps its magnetic property), so they can be separated by physical methods, e.g. by magnetization.

Q: b(i). Iron filings and sulphur powder are heated in a test tube until a black solid is formed. Can you separate the components from this black solid product?

Ans: No. On heating, the iron and sulphur combine chemically and form a new black solid (a compound, iron sulphide). Its components have lost their original properties — the magnet does not attract it — so they cannot be separated by physical methods, only by chemical methods.

Q: b(ii). What does it show?

Ans: It shows that a compound is formed by the chemical combination of elements in a fixed ratio; its components lose their original properties and it can be separated into simpler substances only by chemical methods/reactions.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Air is a mixture of gases: nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and inert (noble) gases, along with water vapours.
  • Nitrogen is present in the maximum amount in air (78%); oxygen is 21% and carbon dioxide is 0.03%.
  • Oxygen is necessary for combustion (burning), rusting and respiration, but not for photosynthesis.
  • Carbon dioxide is used in soft drinks, in fire extinguishers and by plants in photosynthesis.
  • Liquid nitrogen is used as a coolant; oxygen is the gas necessary for the burning process.
  • Inert gases are used in electric bulbs, sign boards and weather balloons.

Solved Exercises

Exercise B: Select the best answer:

Q: 1. Which of these gases are present in maximum amount in air?

Options: (a) oxygen (b) nitrogen (c) chlorine (d) carbon dioxide

Correct answer: nitrogen

Q: 2. Oxygen is not necessary for?

Options: (a) combustion (b) rusting (c) respiration (d) photosynthesis

Correct answer: photosynthesis

Q: 3. Carbon dioxide is used in?

Options: (a) soft drinks (b) fire Extinguishers (c) photosynthesis (d) all of them

Correct answer: all of them

Q: 4. Which is true for nitrogen?

Options: (a) used as dry ice (b) used as coolant (c) used in respiration (d) used in combustion

Correct answer: used as coolant

Q: 5. What is the volume of oxygen and carbon dioxide in air?

Options: (a) 21% carbon dioxide and 0.03% oxygen (b) 0.03% carbon dioxide and 78% oxygen (c) 78% carbon dioxide and 21% oxygen (d) 0.03% carbon dioxide and 21% oxygen

Correct answer: 0.03% carbon dioxide and 21% oxygen

Q: 6. Inert gases are not used in? (Note: in the book the option letters are printed with 'c' twice by mistake; the options in order are electric bulbs, sign boards, photosynthesis and weather balloons.)

Options: (a) electric bulbs (b) sign boards (c) photosynthesis (d) weather balloons

Correct answer: photosynthesis

Q: 7. Which gas in air is necessary for burning process?

Options: (a) oxygen (b) nitrogen (c) carbon dioxide (d) argon

Correct answer: oxygen

mcqs.q: Which of these gases are present in maximum amount in air?
mcqs.why: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air, which is more than any other gas. Oxygen is about 21% and carbon dioxide only 0.03%.

mcqs.q: Oxygen is not necessary for ______.
mcqs.why: Oxygen is needed for burning (combustion), for rusting and for respiration. Photosynthesis does not need oxygen; plants take in carbon dioxide for it and give out oxygen.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide is used in ______.
options: soft drinks, fire extinguishers and photosynthesis
mcqs.why: Carbon dioxide is used in all three: it is dissolved in soft drinks, filled in fire extinguishers, and used by plants in photosynthesis. (The book's keyed option 'all of them' is written out here in full.)

mcqs.q: Which is true for nitrogen?
mcqs.why: Liquid nitrogen is extremely cold and is used as a coolant. Nitrogen does not take part in respiration or combustion; in fact it slows down burning.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of oxygen and carbon dioxide in air?
mcqs.why: Air contains about 21% oxygen and only 0.03% carbon dioxide. The remaining about 78% is nitrogen.

mcqs.q: Inert gases are not used in ______.

Key Points

  • If the percentage of carbon dioxide in air increases, the natural balance of gases is disturbed and the air becomes unfit and harmful for living things.
  • Carbon dioxide can be reduced by planting more and more trees and by reducing the burning of coal, petroleum and natural gas.
  • Nitrogen of the air slows burning, rusting and decay; liquid nitrogen is used as a coolant; plants use nitrogen as nitrates and animals as proteins.
  • Noble gases are chemically inactive gases present in a very small fraction in air: helium, neon, argon, krypton and xenon; argon is the most abundant (almost 0.9%).
  • Water vapours are present in a variable percentage in air; on cooling they form clouds, rain, snow and fog.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Fill the boxes:

Ans: Diagram (in words): Air is a mixture of gases. The four boxes around 'Air' are filled with the names of its constituent gases: Nitrogen, Oxygen (already filled in the book), Carbon dioxide and Inert (noble) gases. Air also contains water vapours in a variable percentage.

Exercise C: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. What will be the disadvantage if the percentage of carbon dioxide is increased in air?

Ans: Human beings and animals inhale oxygen and exhale carbon dioxide, while plants absorb carbon dioxide to prepare their food during photosynthesis; in this way the balance of carbon dioxide in the air is maintained. If the percentage of carbon dioxide in air is increased, this natural balance will be disturbed. The air will become unfit and harmful for living things, because carbon dioxide neither burns nor helps in burning and living things need oxygen for breathing.

Q: 2. How can we reduce carbon dioxide in the air?

Ans: We can reduce carbon dioxide in the air by planting more and more trees, because plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air and use it in photosynthesis to prepare their food. We should also reduce the burning of carbon-containing fuels like coal, petroleum and natural gas, because their burning is a main source of carbon dioxide.

Q: 3. What will happen if all the trees are cut down?

Ans: If all the trees are cut down, there will be no plants to absorb carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and to release oxygen. The carbon dioxide in the air will keep increasing and the oxygen will decrease, so the balance of gases in the air will be disturbed. Living things will not get enough oxygen to breathe, and animals will also lose their food and shelter which trees provide.

Q: 4. How the nitrogen of the air is used?

Ans: The nitrogen of the air is used in many ways: (i) it slows the burning, rusting and decay processes; (ii) liquid nitrogen is used as a coolant; (iii) animals use nitrogen in the form of proteins; (iv) plants use nitrogen in the form of nitrates (fertilizer); and (v) compounds of nitrogen are used in the preparation of fertilizers, medicine etc.

Q: 5. What are noble gases? Name at least three noble gases which are present in air.

Ans: Air contains some gases in a very small fraction called rare or inert gases. These gases are chemically inactive, so they are also known as noble gases. They are colourless and odourless. The noble gases present in air are helium, neon, argon, krypton and xenon; among them argon is present in the maximum amount (almost 0.9% by volume of air).

Q: 6a. Complete the table: Nitrogen — percent by volume in air and one use.

Ans: Nitrogen — Percent by volume in air: 78%. Use: liquid nitrogen is used as coolant; it also slows burning, rusting and decay, and its compounds are used in fertilizers.

Q: 6b. Complete the table: Oxygen — percent by volume in air and one use.

Ans: Oxygen — Percent by volume in air: 21%. Use: it is essential for breathing (respiration) and for burning.

Q: 6c. Complete the table: Carbon dioxide — percent by volume in air and one use.

Ans: Carbon dioxide — Percent by volume in air: 0.03%. Use: it is used by plants during photosynthesis to prepare their food; it is also used in fire extinguishers and soft drinks.

Q: 6d. Complete the table: Water vapours — percent by volume in air and one use.

Ans: Water vapours — Percent by volume in air: variable percentage. Use: when water vapours are cooled they change back into liquid and appear in the form of clouds, rain, snow and fog, so they support the water cycle.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture with uniform composition; a suspension is heterogeneous, its particles can be seen and settle down on standing.
  • States of solution: solid (brass), liquid (sugar dissolved in water) and gas (air).
  • Water is called the universal solvent because more substances dissolve in water than in any other liquid.
  • Sugar dissolves faster in hot water because heat makes the particles move faster.
  • An unsaturated solution can be converted into a saturated solution by adding more solute until no more dissolves at that temperature.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Fill in the following diagram:

Q: Fill in the diagram of the states of solution with examples.

Ans: Diagram (in words): 'State of Solution' has three branches. (1) Solid — example: Brass (a solid solution of zinc and copper metals). (2) Liquid — example: Sugar dissolved in water. (3) Gas — example: Air (a solution of several gases).

Exercise C: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. Differentiate between suspension and solution.

Ans: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances, which has a uniform composition; the solute dissolves completely in the solvent and its particles cannot be seen. A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture (which does not have a uniform composition) of undissolved solute in a given solvent; the particles of the solute are bigger in size and can be seen with the human eye, they settle down if kept undisturbed for some time, and they can be separated by the process of filtration. For example, salt solution is a solution, while chalk and sand in water are suspensions.

Q: 2. What will be the disadvantage if water was not a universal solvent?

Ans: Water is called the universal solvent because more substances dissolve in water than in any other liquid. Wherever water goes, either through the air (water vapours), the ground (rivers, streams) or through our bodies (blood, food), it dissolves chemicals, minerals and nutrients. If water was not a universal solvent, substances like salts, sugar and alcohols could not be dissolved; our blood could not carry dissolved food and nutrients to the body parts, plants could not take up dissolved minerals, and the many solutions used in daily life, such as juices, drinks and medicines, could not be prepared.

Q: 3. Why sugar will dissolve faster in hot water than ice chilled water?

Ans: According to the particle model, the particles of matter are always in motion and adding heat to matter makes the particles move faster. In hot water the particles move faster than in ice chilled water, so they separate and spread the sugar particles quickly, and the solubility also increases with temperature. Therefore sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in ice chilled water.

Q: 4. How can we convert an unsaturated solution into saturated solution?

Ans: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at a given temperature. To convert it into a saturated solution, keep adding more solute to it, a little at a time, and stir it well to dissolve. Continue until a stage comes when no more solute dissolves at that temperature and the extra solute starts settling at the bottom. The solution is now a saturated solution.

Q: 5. Make a list of some common solutions that you use in your home and state from what they are made up of?

Ans: Some common solutions used at home are: Tea — made of water, sugar, tea and milk. Sugar solution (sharbat) — made of sugar dissolved in water. Salt solution — made of table salt dissolved in water. Fruit juices — solutions and suspensions of fruit material in water. Carbonated (soft) drinks — solutions of carbon dioxide gas in water. Perfumes — non-aqueous solutions in which alcohol is used as solvent.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Potential energy is stored in an object due to its position; kinetic energy is the energy of a body due to its motion.
  • When an electric fan is turned on, electrical energy is converted into mechanical (kinetic) energy.
  • In a swinging pendulum, potential energy and kinetic energy keep changing into each other but the total energy remains constant — the law of conservation of energy.
  • Our body needs energy all the time, even during sleep, for activities, growth and repair.
  • Energy from the sun reaches the Earth's surface as radiation and is absorbed into the environment by conduction and released by convection.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. What energy changes takes place when an electric fan is turned on?

Ans: When an electric fan is turned on, electrical energy is converted into mechanical (kinetic) energy by its motor, which makes the blades of the fan move round. A small part of the electrical energy is also converted into heat and sound energy.

Q: 2. What is the difference between kinetic energy and potential energy?

Ans: The energy which is stored in an object due to its position is called potential energy; for example, a stretched rubber band or a stone raised to a certain height has potential energy. The energy in a body due to its motion is called kinetic energy; for example, moving vehicles, a bullet fired from a gun and a moving ball possess kinetic energy. So potential energy is due to position, while kinetic energy is due to motion.

Q: 3. Conduct a simple experiment to show law of conservation of energy.

Ans: Take a pendulum (a hanging ball) and push it to make to-and-fro motion. When the ball is moving, it has kinetic energy. When the ball reaches the extreme point, it has no more kinetic energy; at the highest extreme point the ball has potential energy. When the ball moves again, the potential energy converts into kinetic energy. The pendulum keeps swinging and changing the form of energy from kinetic to potential and back to kinetic, but the total amount of energy remains constant. This shows the law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be destroyed, it can only change its form.

Q: 4. Why energy is so important in our lives?

Ans: Energy is required for all activities and processes. Our body needs energy all the time: we need energy for walking, running, playing and studying, and energy is also needed when we are asleep. Energy keeps our body warm, it is necessary for the growth of our body and it is also used to repair the damaged parts of the body. All living things and machines use energy to do work, and energy converters like the radio, television and lamp improve the quality of our life.

Q: 5. How energy transfer occur in our environment?

Ans: Animals and human beings store the chemical energy of food and then change this chemical energy into heat and kinetic energy; in the end, the heat and kinetic energy dissipate into the atmosphere. Energy in the form of radiation transfers to the earth's surface from the sun and is absorbed into the environment by the conduction method and is then released into the atmosphere by convection processes. In this way, all types of energies pass through different organisms and in the end dissipate in the atmosphere.

Q: 5. A hand drill consist of two mutually perpendicular ______

mcqs.q: Pulley is a simple machine used to ______ the objects.
mcqs.why: A pulley is a grooved wheel over which a rope passes. It is used to lift objects, for example drawing a bucket of water up from a well.

mcqs.why: The pulley at the top of a flag pole is attached to a fixed support and does not move from its place, so it is a fixed pulley. It only changes the direction of the effort.

mcqs.why: In a moveable pulley the load is shared by the rope, so a greater load can be lifted by applying less effort.

mcqs.why: A hand drill works with two gears fitted at right angles (mutually perpendicular) to each other, which change the direction of rotation.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In a fixed pulley the block is fixed and the pulley only changes the direction of the effort; in a moveable pulley the block moves with the load and less effort is needed.
  • Gear system: a force applied on a small gear turns a larger gear slowly but with great force; a larger gear turns a smaller gear faster but with less force.
  • A fixed pulley fitted at the top of a well is used to lift and lower the bucket of water.
  • Wheel and axle is used in the steering wheel of a vehicle, a screwdriver, the crank on a well, door knobs, water taps and a tricycle.
  • A pulley system reduces the effort needed to lift a heavy load; the greater the number of pulleys, the lesser the effort needed.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. Differentiate between fixed pulley and moveable pulley.

Ans: In a fixed pulley, the block of the pulley is connected to a fixed support and does not change its place. One end of the rope is attached to the object to be lifted and effort is applied at its free end; when the free end is pulled downward with an effort equal to the load, the object is lifted upward. A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the applied effort. In a moveable pulley, the block is not connected to a fixed support and the pulley is free to move. One end of the rope is connected with a fixed support, effort is applied at its free end, and the load is hung from the hook of the block of the pulley. Here two parts of the rope support the load, so the load is divided into two and a greater load can be lifted by applying less effort. A moveable pulley does not change the direction of a force; the applied force and the load move in the same direction.

Q: 2. What are the characteristics of a gear system?

Ans: The characteristics of a gear system are: (i) Gears can transmit rotational force to another gear in the same direction or in opposite direction. (ii) The size and number of teeth on a gear determine its working: a force applied on a small gear will turn the larger gear slowly, with fewer revolutions in a minute, but it will have a great force; on the other hand, a force applied on a larger gear will turn a smaller gear faster but it will have less force. (iii) The speed of the driven shaft depends on the number of teeth in each gear.

Q: 3. Which type of simple machine would be used to lower and lift up the bucket of water in a well?

Ans: A pulley is used to lower and lift up the bucket of water in a well. A fixed pulley is fitted at the top of the well; the bucket is tied to one end of the rope passing over the pulley, and when the free end of the rope is pulled down, the bucket is lifted up. The pulley only changes the direction of the applied effort, which makes it easier to draw water from the well. (The crank arrangement on a well works as a wheel and axle, as shown in the figure of the well in this unit.)

Q: 4. Write some uses of a wheel and axle in our daily life?

Ans: Wheel and axle is used in daily life in the steering wheel of a vehicle (a small force on the outer edge of the wheel provides a bigger force at the axle), in a screwdriver (its broader handle is the wheel and the tip is the axle), in the crank on a well, in a drill machine, in door knobs, roller skates, water taps and a tricycle.

Q: 5. Differentiate between a pulley system and gear system.

Ans: A pulley system is a combination of both fixed and moveable pulleys. A pulley is a grooved wheel over which a rope, belt or cable passes, and the pulley system is used for lifting objects to a certain height; it reduces the amount of effort needed to lift a heavy load, and the greater the number of pulleys in the system, the lesser the effort needed. A gear system is a combination of two or more gears. A gear is a wheel with teeth that mesh with the teeth of another gear, and the gear system is used to transmit or receive force and motion; when one gear drives another, both gears revolve in opposite directions (a third gear, the idler gear, makes them turn in the same direction), and the speed of the driven gear depends on the number of teeth in each gear. Gear systems are used in vehicles, bicycles, wind-up clocks, washing machines and hand drills.
