mcqs.why: In a fixed pulley, the block is connected to a fixed support. The effort needed is equal to the load; the pulley only changes the direction of the applied effort, which makes lifting easier.

mcqs.q: In a moveable pulley, the block of the pulley ______.
options: is free to move with the load
mcqs.why: In a moveable pulley the block is not connected to a fixed support; the pulley is free to move, the load hangs from its hook, and less effort is needed to lift the load.

mcqs.q: A force applied on a small gear will turn a larger gear ______.
options: slowly, with fewer revolutions but great force
mcqs.why: The size and number of teeth determine the working of gears: a small gear driving a larger gear makes it turn slowly, with fewer revolutions in a minute, but with great force.

mcqs.q: The speed of the driven shaft in a gear system depends on ______.
options: the number of teeth in each gear
mcqs.why: One of the characteristics of a gear system given in this unit is that the speed of the driven shaft depends on the number of teeth in each gear.

mcqs.q: Which simple machine is used to lower and lift up the bucket of water in a well?
mcqs.why: A fixed pulley is fitted at the top of the well; the bucket is tied to one end of the rope passing over the pulley, and pulling the free end down lifts the bucket up.

mcqs.q: The crank arrangement on a well works as a ______.
mcqs.why: As shown in the figure of the well in this unit, the crank arrangement on a well works as a wheel and axle: turning the large crank rotates the axle around which the rope winds.

mcqs.q: In a screwdriver, the broader handle acts as the ______ and the tip as the axle.
mcqs.why: A screwdriver is an example of wheel and axle: its broader handle is the wheel and the tip is the axle, so a small turning force on the handle gives a bigger force at the tip.

mcqs.q: In a pulley system, the greater the number of pulleys, ______.
options: the lesser the effort needed to lift a heavy load
the slower the rope moves only
mcqs.why: A pulley system is used for lifting objects to a certain height; it reduces the amount of effort needed, and the greater the number of pulleys in the system, the lesser the effort needed.

mcqs.q: The teeth of one gear ______ with the teeth of another gear.
mcqs.why: A gear is a wheel with teeth that mesh (fit into) the teeth of another gear. Through this meshing, the gear system transmits or receives force and motion.

mcqs.q: The steering wheel of a vehicle is an example of ______.
mcqs.why: The steering wheel works as a wheel and axle: a small force applied on the outer edge of the wheel provides a bigger force at the axle to turn the vehicle.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An instrument used to see distant objects is called a telescope; a microscope produces a large image of a small object.
  • The speed of light is 3 x 10^8 m/s.
  • An image formed by a plane mirror is laterally inverted; the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.
  • A convex mirror always forms a virtual image; a concave mirror converges a parallel beam of light.
  • Mirrors used in car head lights and search lights are concave mirrors.
  • A mirror is not a rough surface; paper, wall and cloth are rough surfaces.

Solved Exercises

Exercise A: Fill in the blanks:

Q: 1. An instrument used to see distant objects is called ______.

Ans: telescope

Q: 2. Speed of light is ______.

Ans: 3 x 10^8 m/s

Q: 3. Image formed in concave mirror is always ______.

Ans: real and inverted (when the object is at or beyond the principal focus; if the object is between the focus and the mirror, the image is virtual, upright and magnified)

Q: 4. Image formed by plane mirror is ______ inverted.

Ans: laterally

Q: 5. The angle of incidence is always ______ to the angle of reflection.

Ans: equal

Exercise B: Select the best answer:

Q: 1. Image formed by convex mirror is always ______.

Options: (a) virtual (b) erect and large (c) real (d) inverted

Correct answer: virtual

Q: 2. Concave mirror has the capability to ______ a parallel beam of light.

Options: (a) converge (b) diverge (c) dispense (d) no change

Correct answer: converge

Q: 3. A microscope is an instrument used to produce a ______ image:

Options: (a) large (b) small (c) short (d) far

Correct answer: large

Q: 4. Which one is not a rough surface:

Options: (a) paper (b) wall (c) cloth (d) mirror

Correct answer: mirror

Q: 5. Mirrors used in car head lights and search lights are ______.

Options: (a) convex (b) concave (c) plane (d) all of them

Correct answer: concave

Exercise C: Match column A with column B:

Q: Multiple reflection

Ans: Kaleidoscope (multiple reflection is the phenomenon used in a kaleidoscope, where a number of images of an object are formed by two plane mirrors inclined to each other).

Q: Periscope

Ans: Two plane mirrors (a simple periscope is constructed by using two plane mirrors at 45 degrees in a tube).

Q: Microscope

Ans: Large image (a microscope is used to produce a large image of a small object like bacteria).

Q: Pinhole camera

Ans: Real image (the image formed by a pinhole camera is a real one).

Q: Convex mirror

Ans: Virtual image (a convex mirror always forms an upright, virtual and smaller image).

mcqs.q: Image formed by convex mirror is always ______.
mcqs.why: A convex mirror always forms an upright, virtual and smaller image. It can never form a real image on a screen.

mcqs.q: Concave mirror has the capability to ______ a parallel beam of light.
mcqs.why: A concave mirror is a converging mirror: it brings a parallel beam of light together (converges it) at its focus. That is why concave mirrors are used in search lights and head lights.

mcqs.why: A microscope is used to produce a large image of a very small object, like bacteria, so that it can be studied.

mcqs.why: Car head lights and search lights use concave mirrors, which converge light into a strong parallel beam. (The book's printed option 'all of them' is replaced here by 'cylindrical', since only the concave mirror does this job.)

mcqs.q: An instrument used to see distant objects is called ______.
mcqs.why: A telescope is the instrument used to see distant objects, such as stars and planets, clearly and enlarged.

mcqs.q: Speed of light is ______.
mcqs.why: Light travels at a speed of 3 x 10^8 metres per second in vacuum, which is much faster than the speed of sound in air (about 340 m/s).

mcqs.q: Image formed by a plane mirror is ______ inverted.
mcqs.why: A plane mirror forms an image that is laterally inverted: the left side of the object appears on the right side in the image, and vice versa.

mcqs.q: When the object is at or beyond the principal focus, the image formed by a concave mirror is ______.
mcqs.why: The solved answer of this unit states that the image formed in a concave mirror is real and inverted when the object is at or beyond the principal focus; if the object is between the focus and the mirror, the image is virtual, upright and magnified.

mcqs.q: The image formed by a pinhole camera is a ______ image.
mcqs.why: The matching exercise of this unit pairs the pinhole camera with a real image: the image formed by a pinhole camera is real and inverted.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright image of equal size; a pinhole camera forms a real, inverted and mostly smaller image.
  • Dark clothes absorb more light and produce more heat, so people wear dark clothes in winter; white clothes reflect most light, so they are worn in summer.
  • Transmission: light passes through transparent objects. Absorption: light is taken in by an opaque surface and creates heat. Reflection: light bounces back from a smooth shiny surface.
  • A kaleidoscope works on multiple reflection; a periscope is made of two plane mirrors; a convex mirror forms an upright, virtual and smaller image.

Solved Exercises

Exercise D: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. Compare the images formed by a plane mirror and pinhole camera.

Ans: A plane mirror forms a virtual image, while a pinhole camera forms a real image. A plane mirror forms the image of equal size as of the object, while a pinhole camera mostly forms smaller or diminished images. A plane mirror forms an upright image, while a pinhole camera forms an inverted image.

Q: 2. Mostly people wear white clothes in summer and dark clothes in winter season. Give reason.

Ans: When a ray of light strikes an opaque surface, some of it gets absorbed and the energy from the light is transferred to the surface material, which creates heat. Dark clothes absorb more light, so more heat is produced and the body stays warm; therefore people wear dark clothes in the winter season. White clothes absorb very little light and reflect most of it, so the body stays cool; therefore people wear white clothes in summer.

Q: 3. Differentiate between the transmission, absorption and reflection of light.

Ans: Transmission of light: light passes through transparent objects easily, for example glass and some plastic sheets; the passage of light through a transparent object is called transmission of light. Absorption of light: when a ray of light strikes an opaque surface, some of it gets absorbed; the energy from the light is transferred to the surface material and this transfer creates a small amount of heat; such behaviour of light is called absorption of light. Reflection of light: when light falls on a smooth shiny object, like a mirror, it bounces back in one particular direction; this bouncing of light is called reflection of light.

Q: 4. Prove the law of reflection through an activity.

Ans: Take a drawing board and fix a white paper on it with a drawing pin. Place a mirror slab XY (fixed in standing position) on the white paper. Fix two common pins N and M obliquely in front of the mirror in a straight line. Look at the image of the pins in the mirror and fix two more common pins Q and R in such a way that the images of pins N and M and pins Q and R lie on the same straight line. Join all the points N, M, Q and R with the mirror XY at point P, and draw a normal at point P. Measure the angle of incidence NPS, which the incident ray NM forms with the normal, and the angle of reflection RPS, which the reflected ray QR forms with the normal. The two angles are found equal. This proves the law of reflection: the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection (and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane).

mcqs.q: Compare: a plane mirror forms a ______ image, while a pinhole camera forms a real image.
mcqs.why: A plane mirror forms a virtual image (which cannot be taken on a screen), while a pinhole camera forms a real image. The plane mirror image is upright and of equal size; the pinhole image is inverted and mostly smaller.

mcqs.q: People wear dark clothes in the winter season because dark clothes ______.
options: absorb more light, so more heat is produced
mcqs.why: When light strikes an opaque surface, some of it is absorbed and its energy creates heat. Dark clothes absorb more light, so more heat is produced and the body stays warm in winter.

mcqs.q: People wear white clothes in summer because white clothes ______.
options: absorb very little light and reflect most of it
mcqs.why: White clothes absorb very little light and reflect most of it, so very little heat is produced and the body stays cool in summer.

mcqs.q: The passage of light through a transparent object, like glass, is called ______.
mcqs.why: Light passes through transparent objects easily, for example glass and some plastic sheets. This passage of light through a transparent object is called transmission of light.

mcqs.q: When light falls on a smooth shiny object like a mirror and bounces back in one particular direction, this is called ______.
mcqs.why: Reflection of light is the bouncing back of light in one particular direction when it falls on a smooth shiny object like a mirror.

mcqs.q: A kaleidoscope works on the phenomenon of ______.
mcqs.why: In a kaleidoscope, two plane mirrors inclined to each other form a number of images of an object. This phenomenon is called multiple reflection.

mcqs.q: A simple periscope is constructed by using ______.
options: two plane mirrors at 45 degrees in a tube
mcqs.why: The matching exercise of this unit pairs the periscope with two plane mirrors: a simple periscope is constructed by using two plane mirrors at 45 degrees in a tube.

mcqs.q: A convex mirror always forms an image that is ______.
mcqs.why: The matching exercise of this unit states that a convex mirror always forms an upright, virtual and smaller image, which is why it is used as a driving mirror.

mcqs.q: In the law of reflection experiment with pins and a mirror, the measured angle of incidence is ______ the angle of reflection.
mcqs.why: In the activity, the angle of incidence NPS and the angle of reflection are measured with the normal drawn at point P, and they are found equal. This proves the law of reflection: the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.

mcqs.q: Absorption of light takes place when light strikes ______.
mcqs.why: When a ray of light strikes an opaque surface, some of it gets absorbed; the energy from the light is transferred to the surface material and this transfer creates a small amount of heat.

Key Points

  • The speed of sound in iron is 5130 m/s; sound travels as longitudinal waves.

mcqs.q: Sound cannot travel through ______.
mcqs.why: Sound needs a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel. There is no medium in a vacuum, so sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

mcqs.q: Human ear has ______ distinct parts.
mcqs.why: The human ear has three distinct parts: the outer ear, the middle ear and the inner ear.

mcqs.q: Speed of sound ______ in air with increase in temperature.

mcqs.q: Speed of sound in Iron is ______.
mcqs.why: Sound travels fastest in solids. Its speed in iron is 5130 m/s, which is much faster than in water (about 1525 m/s) and in air (about 340 m/s).

mcqs.q: The sound is a form of energy which travel through any medium as ______.
mcqs.why: Sound travels through a medium as longitudinal waves, made of compressions and rarefactions travelling one after the other.

mcqs.q: Sound waves cannot pass through ______.

mcqs.q: Sound is also a form of ______.
mcqs.why: Sound does work as it travels from one place to another through a medium, so sound is a form of energy associated with the vibrations of matter.

mcqs.q: Human ear can detect frequency from 20 hertz to ______ hertz.
mcqs.why: Hearing takes place when vibrations of frequencies ranging from 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz reach the inner ear. This is the hearing range of a human being.

mcqs.q: Back and forth movement of an object is called ______.
mcqs.why: The back and forth movement of an object is called vibration. Sound is produced when an object vibrates.

mcqs.why: The speed of sound in air greatly varies with temperature: it increases as the temperature of the air increases.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Sound is produced by a vibrating body; a vibrating tuning fork can throw away a pith-ball, which proves sound is a form of energy.
  • Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases: iron 5130 m/s, water about 1525 m/s, air 332 m/s at 0°C and 340 m/s at 20°C.
  • The human ear has three distinct parts: outer ear, middle ear and inner ear; the eardrum vibrates when sound waves strike it.
  • Safety measures: do not enter any object into the ear, and do not try to listen to sounds of very high frequency.

Solved Exercises

Exercise D: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. Prove that sound is a form of energy.

Ans: We know that when something moves, work is done. Sound travels from one place to another through a medium, so it does work; thus sound is the form of energy that moves and is associated with the vibrations or disturbances of matter. For example, when a vibrating tuning fork is touched with a pith-ball, the ball is thrown away by the vibrations, and sound energy is so strong that some of the sound frequencies can even break glass windows. This proves that sound is a form of energy.

Q: 2. How sound is produced. Explain with examples.

Ans: Sound is produced by a vibrating body. Vibrations mean the back and forth movement of an object. For example, when you strike a metallic object with a spoon, a sound is produced and you can feel the vibrations by touching the metallic object with your hand. When the volume of a cassette player is high, the sheet of the loudspeaker vibrates very fast and produces loud sound. Similarly, if we touch our throat while we are talking, we can feel the vibrations in our voice box. A rubber chord fixed between two hooks also produces sound when it is plucked, because it vibrates. Thus sound is produced when an object vibrates.

Q: 3. Compare the speed of sound in solids, liquids and gaseous media.

Ans: Sound generally moves much faster in liquids and solids than in gases. The speed of sound in dry, sea level air at a temperature of 0°C is 332 m/s, and at 20°C it is 340 m/s. The speed of sound in water is approximately 1525 m/s, which is almost five times as fast as in the air. The speed of sound in iron (solid) is 5130 m/s, which is much faster than in water (liquid) and air (gas). So sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.

Q: 4. Explain how does human ear receive sound waves.

Ans: The process of hearing begins when sound waves strike upon an ear. The human ear has three distinct parts: the outer ear, the middle ear and the inner ear. The outer ear collects the sound waves and directs them along the ear canal to the eardrum, which is caused to vibrate. The message of these vibrations is sent to the brain. The brain interprets this message as the sensation of the sound. Hearing takes place whenever vibrations of frequencies ranging from 20 Hertz to 20,000 Hertz reach the inner ear.

Q: 5. Write down any two safety measures, which will protect your ear drum from the damage.

Ans: Two safety measures to protect the eardrum are: (i) Do not enter any object into the ear, because the eardrum is very sensitive and can be easily damaged. (ii) Do not try to listen to the sound which has high frequency, and do all the activities related to sound production carefully.

mcqs.q: Sound is produced by ______.
mcqs.why: Sound is produced by a vibrating body. When you strike a metallic object with a spoon, it vibrates and produces sound, and the vibrations can be felt by touching it.

mcqs.q: When a vibrating tuning fork is touched with a pith-ball, the ball is thrown away. This proves that ______.
options: sound is a form of energy
mcqs.why: The vibrating fork does work on the pith-ball and throws it away. Sound travels and does work, so sound is the form of energy associated with vibrations of matter; strong sound can even break glass windows.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound in dry air at 20°C is ______.
mcqs.why: The speed of sound in dry, sea level air is 332 m/s at 0°C and 340 m/s at 20°C, because the speed of sound in air increases with temperature.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound in water is approximately ______.
mcqs.why: The speed of sound in water is approximately 1525 m/s, which is almost five times as fast as in air.

mcqs.q: Sound travels fastest in ______.
mcqs.why: Sound generally moves much faster in liquids and solids than in gases: fastest in solids (iron 5130 m/s), slower in liquids (water 1525 m/s) and slowest in gases (air about 340 m/s).

mcqs.q: The process of hearing begins when sound waves strike upon ______.
mcqs.why: Hearing begins when sound waves strike an ear. The outer ear collects the waves and directs them along the ear canal to the eardrum, which is caused to vibrate.

mcqs.why: The vibrations of the eardrum pass through the ear to the inner ear, and their message is sent to the brain. The brain interprets this message as the sensation of sound.

options: enter a pin into the ear to clean it
do not enter any object into the ear
listen to very loud sounds daily

mcqs.why: Talking produces sound because the voice box vibrates. Touching the throat while talking lets us feel these vibrations, which shows that sound is produced by a vibrating body.

mcqs.why: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because there is no medium in it, so a vacuum is matched with 'no sound' in this unit's matching exercise.

Key Points

Key Points

  • Telecommunication satellites carry radio, T.V. and telephone signals over long distances; the GPS, a group of 24 satellites, enables a person to determine his location, speed, direction and time anywhere.
  • Satellites are of two major types: natural satellites (like the Earth's moon) and artificial satellites (objects launched into orbit by human beings).
  • Asteroids are rocky bodies up to 1000 km in diameter moving in elliptical orbits between Mars and Jupiter.
  • Comets are small icy bodies with a head, a coma and a long luminous tail when near the Sun.
  • Kinds of meteors: brilliant meteors (fireballs), bolides (which explode with a sound like thunder) and fainter meteors (shooting stars); a cluster of meteors from a fixed point is called a meteor shower.

Solved Exercises

Exercise C: Answer the following questions:

Q: 1. Describe the uses of various satellites in space.

Ans: Scientists have developed many kinds of satellites, each designed to serve a specific purpose or mission. Telecommunications satellites help in carrying radio, T.V. and telephone signals over long distances, and communication satellites link remote areas of earth with telephone and television. Navigational satellites pinpoint the location of objects on Earth; the Global Positioning System (GPS), a group of 24 satellites, enables a person to determine his location, speed, direction and time anywhere. Weather satellites help in weather forecast, and polar satellites provide weather information and also map ozone levels. Surveillance satellites are used to monitor military activities. Scientific satellites give a space based platform for observation of Earth, the other planets, the Sun, the comets, the galaxies and the outer space. Landsat satellites have taken photographs of earth's continents and surrounding coastal regions, and their data is used for mapping land, managing forested land, estimating crop production and protecting wild life.

Q: 2. Define satellites. Classify the satellites into its major types.

Ans: Any heavenly body that revolves around the planets is known as a satellite. Satellites are classified into two major types: (1) Natural satellites: in astronomy, a celestial body that revolves around a planet is known as a natural satellite; the best known natural satellite is the Earth's moon, and other planets also have moons. Beside moons of planets, some other bodies (natural satellites) are asteroids, comets and meteoroids, which are moving around the sun. (2) Artificial satellites: an object launched into orbit by human beings is called an artificial satellite; it revolves around the Earth or other planets. The first artificial satellite was launched in 1957. Artificial satellites play a key role in communications, industry, military intelligence and in the scientific study of the Earth and outer space.

Q: 3. Differentiate between Asteroids, Comets and Meteors.

Ans: Asteroids: size up to 1000 km in diameter; shape irregular; composition carbon, iron and other metals; location between Mars and Jupiter. They are rocky bodies of different sizes that move in elliptical orbits between Mars and Jupiter. Comets: size up to 20 km in diameter; shape irregular; composition iron, rock, ammonia and other gases; they move in elliptical orbit around the sun. They are relatively small, icy celestial bodies revolving around the Sun, with a head, a coma and a long luminous tail when near the Sun. Meteors: size from few centimeters to few meters in diameter; shape irregular; composition iron, rock, etc.; they are the wandering bodies in the solar system. A meteor is a small solid body made up of rocks and iron which burns with light when it enters the Earth's atmosphere.

Q: 4. Explain the different kinds of meteors.

Ans: The different kinds of meteors are: (1) Brilliant meteors: they are known as fireballs; they occur singly and consist of a luminous head, followed by a tail of light. (2) Bolides: these are the kind of meteors that have been seen to explode with a sound like thunder. (3) Fainter meteors: they are called shooting or falling stars. We usually can see several of them on a clear starry night; sometimes hundreds of such meteors occur simultaneously and appear from a fixed point, and this cluster of meteors is called meteor showers. (A few meteors, the very large ones, sometimes strike the surface of the earth; they are called meteorites.)
